notes.meaning: Dinah was Jacob's only daughter, born to Leah. She was likely a young teen, about fourteen to sixteen. She went out to meet the young women of the land, perhaps at one of their festivals. Older writers saw a warning here for parents to watch over their children with care.

Shechem was the son of Hamor, the local chief. He saw Dinah, seized her, and raped her. Clarke and Calvin point out that the story shows she did not agree to it. It was an act of violence, and she was then kept in his house.

Afterward Shechem grew attached to Dinah. He "spoke to her heart," trying to comfort her and win her with the promise of marriage. Unlike some men, he did not cast her aside, and he asked his father to arrange the marriage. Still, Calvin says he had sinned gravely by giving in to his lust first.

Jacob heard the news but said nothing until his sons came home. He may have been crushed by grief, or he may have waited so he would not act alone. In that culture, a girl's full brothers were expected to protect her and avenge wrongs against her. Matthew Henry also wonders if Jacob had let his sons run things too much.

Hamor came to talk with Jacob just as the sons returned, full of grief and anger. "An outrage in Israel" became a common phrase for shameful sins among God's people. Jacob had been renamed Israel, so this was seen as a wrong against God's chosen family. Yet the commentators warn that their anger went too far, since no injury gives us the right to take revenge.

Hamor made a generous offer: marriage, the families marrying each other, and freedom to live, trade, and own land. Matthew Henry and Wesley say that here the Canaanites seem more honest than Jacob's sons. But Hamor and Shechem never said they were sorry. They also did not send Dinah home.

Shechem begged to marry Dinah and offered any price they named. The "dowry" was a gift for the bride. The "gift" meant presents for her family. Clarke says Shechem was trying to make what amends he could.

Jacob's sons answered with a lie, angry because their sister had been wronged. Circumcision was the sign of God's covenant, His binding promise to Abraham's family. They were right that they should not marry outside God's people. But they used this holy sign as a cover for a cruel plan, which made their sin far worse.

The brothers said that every man in the city must be circumcised before the families could become one people. Matthew Henry says they wanted the men sore, not holy. They never taught the city to worship the true God, only to take the outward sign. Their threat to "take our sister and go" shows Dinah was still being held.

Hamor and Shechem liked the terms. Shechem acted quickly because he loved Dinah, and as the most respected man in his family, he set the example. Henry and Wesley suggest they may also have heard something about the honor of this sign in Abraham's family.

The city gate was where people gathered and where cases were judged. Hamor and Shechem praised Jacob's family as peaceful and said the land had plenty of room. Calvin notes that they hid their real, private reason. Leaders often claim to serve the public good while seeking their own gain.

They named the condition and then dangled a reward: Jacob's flocks and wealth would become theirs. Matthew Henry sees greed as the real matchmaker here. To take on a religious sign just to get rich was even worse. Clarke calls it bait for the people.

Every man in the city agreed and was circumcised. This shows either great love for their leaders or the total power of chiefs in that region. Calvin says they changed religion lightly, for gain and without real conviction.

On the third day, while the men were in pain and helpless, Simeon and Levi attacked. They were Dinah's full brothers and probably led their servants with them. They killed every man in the city. Wesley says nothing can excuse it: one man had sinned, the whole town paid, and the deed was done through betrayal of a sworn agreement.
They killed Hamor and Shechem and took Dinah from Shechem's house. Matthew Henry points out that they could have gotten her back without bloodshed, as their own words in verse 17 show.

Jacob's other sons joined in and looted the city, taking animals, goods, women, and children. By doing so they shared in the guilt. Calvin says one sin quickly led to another, as killers turned into robbers. Matthew Henry notes the irony: the city hoped to gain Jacob's wealth, but lost its own.

Jacob rebuked Simeon and Levi for making his family hated by their neighbors, since they were few and could be wiped out. He spoke of the danger, perhaps because that was what would reach his hard-hearted sons. His words on his deathbed (Genesis 49:5-7) show he hated what they did. Only God's protection kept the family safe (Genesis 35:5).

The brothers defended themselves with a sharp question. Matthew Henry answers: no, Shechem should not have treated Dinah that way, but that did not make them free to take revenge on a whole city. Calvin urges us to leave vengeance to God. Clarke notes that Scripture tells this dark story honestly, with blame on all sides.
